chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
title: Draft status, USO plans and the recording ban
summary: McRae was a family man and cannot recall how he avoided the draft; his brothers went on the USO and Shaw's Navy band, and Lunceford made no records.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: Well you were with Jimmy Lunceford then during the recording ban. Do you remember when that took effect -- the ban on recording?

During the war. Let's back up a bit. You were -- when they started drafting -- well I guess you were about thirty-three years old so, were you considered too old to be drafted or because -- Because I think they were drafting what they call "able bodied men" up to thirty-five, but you had a family too. I had a family. And then -- I think I was working a lot. I think I was travelling a lot, or something. I didn't -- who got me out of that? Somebody got me out of that. Can't think who it was now. Something I was doing and we decided that we would do something for the Army (inaudible). Because a lot of musicians went to California, then got in a band out there.
Did they get into the USO activities?
My brother went in the USO. My other brother, Bob, took Artie Shaw's place with the band. He went out there and Artie Shaw's
